heroHeadline: DHS Shuts Down Detention Watchdog (OIDO); 11th Circuit Strikes Down Mandatory No-Bond Detention; Senate Advances $71.7B Enforcement Package
heroSubtitle: On May 5, 2026, DHS shut down the Office of Immigration Detention Ombudsman (OIDO) — the independent watchdog Congress created in the 2019 NDAA to investigate abuse in ICE detention. Critics including legal scholars say DHS's claim that Congress defunded OIDO is false; the appropriations law contains no repeal language. The closure removes the sole independent oversight mechanism for a detention system with 30+ FY2026 custody deaths. On May 6, the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals struck down Trump's mandatory no-bond detention policy — the second appeals court to do so (after the 2nd Circuit on April 29), creating a four-circuit split that makes Supreme Court review near-certain. Senate committees also advanced a $71.7 billion immigration enforcement reconciliation bill (ICE: ~$38.2B; CBP: ~$26.1B) with a floor vote targeted for the week of May 18 and a Trump-imposed June 1 signing deadline. This follows ICE paying local police $100,000+ in vehicles to join 287(g) agreements (now 1,786 MOAs covering 32% of the U.S. population), documented chemical agent use on civil detainees (WaPo, May 4), and the WEXMAC military contracting tool being used to convert buildings into detention centers while bypassing public review.
footerNote: Data sourced from DHS, ICE official records, ACLU, HRW, DHS OIG, TRAC Reports, Detention Watch Network, court records, and Congressional records
